headline: August 27: Washington's Early Start Is Still Paying Rent
subhead: The same warm-water setup that got Washington going ahead of the pack in June is still holding late in August, and the canyon is fishing like it knows it.
body_markdown:
Late August is usually when a lot of the Mid-Atlantic canyons start showing their age for the season — the early push fades, the water cools a half-degree here and there, and the bite gets choppier. Washington doesn't play by that calendar, and this year is no different. This canyon typically gets its warm-water setup earlier than its neighbors because of where it sits relative to the Gulf Stream, and that head start built in June is still paying dividends heading into September. The regime that's been in place — stable high pressure, southwest winds sitting in that 8-to-12 knot window, warm water holding firm — hasn't broken down. That's the story of the last several days and it's the story for the next few, too.

What that means practically is the canyon is still fishing like mid-summer instead of easing into the fall turn. Yellowfin remain the bread-and-butter species working the temperature breaks and current edges, white marlin are still showing on the troll where the water color changes, and mahi are scattered around whatever floating structure and weed lines the fleet can find. It's not a banner week where every boat limits out — it's a solid, honest mixed-bag week, and that's worth saying plainly. Some days the walls are stacked with life and some days boats have to run and hunt before they find the right piece of water. That's normal for this stretch of the season. The fish are here; they're just not evenly distributed, and that's exactly what you'd expect with a warm-water regime that's held steady rather than one that's actively pushing new water and new bait into the canyon.

The pattern that's produced the best results has been working the temperature and color breaks along the eastern and western walls rather than blind-trolling open water. Boats anchoring up on bait schools holding tight to the edges have done well chunking butterfish and bunker chunks, drawing yellowfin up out of the deeper water into a chum slick worked over a couple hours of tide. That bite tends to build slow and then go off in a short window, so patience at anchor has been outproducing boats that keep picking up and moving every 20 minutes. On the troll, a standard spread of naked and skirted ballyhoo behind small to mid-size bird teasers has been the go-to for both yellowfin and white marlin, with marlin especially responsive to a dink ballyhoo pulled just off a spreader bar in that flat, glassy water that builds under the current high pressure. Wahoo have shown up as a bycatch on the high-speed gear — boards or planers pulling cedar plugs and small skirted lures at 12-plus knots along the drop-offs — but they've been more opportunistic than a targeted, reliable bite this week.

Mahi have been the wildcard, and honestly the most fun part of the report. Anywhere the fleet has found a real weed line or a patch of floating debris, there have been fish stacked underneath it — some short, some pushing better than 10 pounds. Small hookless teasers followed by spinning tackle pitching pilchards or a bit of chunk bait has been the standard approach, and it's produced some of the more consistent action of the week when the bigger pelagics went quiet for a stretch. If there's one thing worth telling anyone headed out — carry the spinning rods rigged and ready, because the mahi bite has been the difference between a mediocre day and a genuinely good one more than once this week.

The bigger picture explains why this is holding. Washington sits in a warm-water regime that's been stable for days now, and there's no sign of that breaking in the near term. High pressure isn't going anywhere fast, the southwest wind pattern keeps the surface calm enough for good trolling conditions, and the warm water that's been in place isn't showing the kind of cooling that starts to push these pelagics off the canyon edge. That's the Washington advantage again — this canyon got its warm-water setup weeks before some of its neighbors, and it's simply got more runway left before any seasonal cooling starts to matter.

Looking at the next few days, expect more of the same conditions-wise — steady high pressure, manageable southwest wind, warm water holding. The moon is building toward full, which should tighten up the current on the walls and sharpen the bite windows rather than spread them out, so boats that time their drift or anchor to the peak of the tide swing should see better concentrated action than boats fishing the slack. Longer range, there's some early chatter about cooler nights starting to nudge water temperatures down farther north, but that's a story for New England and the Sound right now, not for Washington. This canyon's warm-water window still has room to run. If there's only one day to make the trip this week, work the walls on the building tide around the moon, keep the chunk bags ready for the yellowfin, and don't leave the spinning rods below — the mahi have been too good to leave on the dock.
